intro.title: A to-do list engine
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Every to-do app has the same engine inside: tasks that can be added, ticked off, tagged, given a due date, saved and shown. In this capstone you build that engine in plain JavaScript, piece by piece. A web page or phone app could then sit on top of it.

It uses most of the course: **classes** for tasks and the list, **regular expressions** to read quick-add text like `Buy milk #home due:2026-11-20`, **array methods** for the views, **JSON** to save and load, and **dates** in `YYYY-MM-DD` text for what is due.

```text
Overdue
  [ ] Buy milk #home (2026-11-10)
Today
  [x] Send report #work
Later
  [ ] Book dentist (2026-12-01)
No date
  [ ] Read a book #home
```

Each challenge gives you the code built so far, so you can focus on the new piece. Keep the habits from the last quests: small methods that do one thing, data that can be saved as JSON, and the showing kept apart from the logic.

A tip for working on a bigger program: after each piece, try it on a tiny example in the sandbox before moving on. Bugs are easy to find in ten new lines and hard to find in a hundred.

challenges.title: Easy: A task
challenges.promptMarkdown: Write `class Task` with a constructor `(id, title)` that sets `id`, `title`, `done` (`false`), `tags` (`[]`) and `due` (`null`), a method `toggle()` that flips `done`, and `toString()` that gives `[ ] TITLE`, or `[x] TITLE` when done.
challenges.hint: `return `[${this.done ? "x" : " "}] ${this.title}``.

tests.label: A new task
tests.assertion: (() => { const t = new Task(1, "Walk"); return t.id === 1 && t.done === false && t.due === null && Array.isArray(t.tags) && t.toString() === "[ ] Walk" })()

tests.label: Toggle
tests.assertion: (() => { const t = new Task(1, "Walk"); t.toggle(); const a = t.toString(); t.toggle(); return a === "[x] Walk" && t.done === false })()

challenges.title: Easy: Read quick-add text
challenges.promptMarkdown: Write `parseTask(text)` that returns `{ title, tags, due }`: the tags are the words after `#` (without it), `due` the date after `due:` (or `null`), and the title is the rest, with single spaces and no spaces at the ends.
challenges.hint: `matchAll(/#(\w+)/g)` for tags, `match(/due:(\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2})/)` for the date, then remove both from the text with `replace(/#\w+|due:\S+/g, "")` and tidy the spaces.

tests.label: Everything
tests.assertion: JSON.stringify(parseTask("Buy milk #home due:2026-11-20 #shop")) === JSON.stringify({ title: "Buy milk", tags: ["home", "shop"], due: "2026-11-20" })

tests.label: Just a title
tests.assertion: JSON.stringify(parseTask("  Call   Mum ")) === JSON.stringify({ title: "Call Mum", tags: [], due: null })

challenges.title: Easy: Add tasks
challenges.promptMarkdown: Write `class TaskList` with `tasks` (empty) and `nextId` (1), and `add(text)` that parses the text, makes a `Task` with the next id, sets its `tags` and `due`, adds it and returns it.
challenges.hint: `const task = new Task(this.nextId++, title)`, then set `tags` and `due`.

tests.label: Ids go up
tests.assertion: (() => { const l = new TaskList(); const a = l.add("One"); const b = l.add("Two #x"); return a.id === 1 && b.id === 2 && l.tasks.length === 2 && b.tags[0] === "x" && b instanceof Task })()

challenges.title: Medium: Find and remove
challenges.promptMarkdown: Add `find(id)` (throws `Error("No task ID")` if there is none) and `remove(id)` (also throws for an unknown id) to `TaskList`.
challenges.hint: `find` uses `this.tasks.find`; `remove` calls `this.find(id)` first (so it throws), then filters.

tests.label: Find
tests.assertion: (() => { const l = new TaskList(); l.add("A"); l.add("B"); return l.find(2).title === "B" })()

tests.label: Remove
tests.assertion: (() => { const l = new TaskList(); l.add("A"); l.add("B"); l.remove(1); return l.tasks.map((t) => t.title).join() === "B" })()

tests.label: Unknown id
tests.assertion: (() => { try { new TaskList().remove(9) } catch (_cq_e) { return (String(_cq_e?.name) + ": " + String(_cq_e?.message)).includes("No task 9") } return false })()

tests.label: Works with other data too

challenges.title: Medium: Views
challenges.promptMarkdown: Add `active()` and `completed()` (the tasks not done and done), and `summary()` giving text like `1 of 4 done`.
challenges.hint: Two `filter`s, and `` `${this.completed().length} of ${this.tasks.length} done` ``.

tests.label: Views
tests.assertion: (() => { const list = new TaskList(); list.add("Buy milk #home due:2026-11-10"); list.add("Send report #work due:2026-11-12"); list.add("Book dentist due:2026-12-01"); list.add("Read a book #home"); list.find(2).toggle();  return list.active().length === 3 && list.completed()[0].title === "Send report" })()

tests.label: Summary
tests.assertion: (() => { const list = new TaskList(); list.add("Buy milk #home due:2026-11-10"); list.add("Send report #work due:2026-11-12"); list.add("Book dentist due:2026-12-01"); list.add("Read a book #home"); list.find(2).toggle();  return list.summary() === "1 of 4 done" })()

tests.label: Works with other data too

challenges.title: Medium: By tag
challenges.promptMarkdown: Write `byTag(list)` that returns an object of tag → the titles of the tasks with that tag, in the order added.
challenges.hint: Loop over `list.tasks` and their `tags`; push the title into `groups[tag]` (starting with `[]`).

tests.label: The sample
tests.assertion: JSON.stringify(byTag(list)) === JSON.stringify({ home: ["Buy milk", "Read a book"], work: ["Send report"] })

tests.label: Empty
tests.assertion: JSON.stringify(byTag(new TaskList())) === JSON.stringify({})

tests.label: Works with other data too

challenges.title: Hard: What is overdue
challenges.promptMarkdown: Write `overdue(list, today)` that returns the titles of tasks that are **not done** and have a due date before `today` (`YYYY-MM-DD` text), oldest due date first.
challenges.hint: Filter on `!t.done && t.due !== null && t.due < today`, sort by `due` with `localeCompare`, map to titles.

tests.label: 12 November
tests.assertion: JSON.stringify(overdue(list, "2026-11-12")) === JSON.stringify(["Buy milk"])

tests.label: Later
tests.assertion: JSON.stringify(overdue(list, "2026-12-25")) === JSON.stringify(["Buy milk", "Book dentist"])

tests.label: Works with other data too

challenges.title: Hard: Save and load
challenges.promptMarkdown: Add `toJSON()` to `TaskList` returning `{ nextId, tasks }` (tasks as plain objects), and a static `fromJSON(text)` that builds a working `TaskList` back from that JSON text, with real `Task` objects.
challenges.hint: `toJSON() { return { nextId: this.nextId, tasks: this.tasks.map((t) => ({ ...t })) } }`. In `fromJSON`, parse, make a list, and `Object.assign(new Task(d.id, d.title), d)` for each task.

tests.label: Round trip
tests.assertion: (() => { const list = new TaskList(); list.add("Buy milk #home due:2026-11-10"); list.add("Send report #work due:2026-11-12"); list.add("Book dentist due:2026-12-01"); list.add("Read a book #home"); list.find(2).toggle();  const back = TaskList.fromJSON(JSON.stringify(list)); return back instanceof TaskList && back.tasks.length === 4 && back.tasks[1] instanceof Task && back.tasks[1].done === true && back.tasks[0].due === "2026-11-10" && back.find(4).tags[0] === "home" })()

tests.label: Ids carry on
tests.assertion: (() => { const list = new TaskList(); list.add("Buy milk #home due:2026-11-10"); list.add("Send report #work due:2026-11-12"); list.add("Book dentist due:2026-12-01"); list.add("Read a book #home"); list.find(2).toggle();  const back = TaskList.fromJSON(JSON.stringify(list)); return back.add("New").id === 5 })()

tests.label: Works with other data too

challenges.title: Expert: Undo
challenges.promptMarkdown: Write `class UndoableList extends TaskList` that remembers the state before every `add`, `remove` and `toggle(id)` (a new method that toggles a task), and has `undo()`, which goes back one step (and does nothing if there is nothing to undo). Save states as JSON text.
challenges.hint: Keep `this.history = []`. A `snapshot()` pushes `JSON.stringify({ nextId: this.nextId, tasks: this.tasks })`. Call it at the start of `add`, `remove` and `toggle`. `undo()` pops the last one and rebuilds `nextId` and `tasks` (as `Task`s) from it.

tests.label: Undo a toggle
tests.assertion: (() => { const l = new UndoableList(); l.add("A"); l.toggle(1); l.undo(); return l.find(1).done === false && l.find(1) instanceof Task })()

tests.label: Undo a remove, then an add
tests.assertion: (() => { const l = new UndoableList(); l.add("A"); l.add("B"); l.remove(1); l.undo(); const back = l.tasks.length === 2; l.undo(); return back && l.tasks.length === 1 && l.add("C").id === 2 })()

tests.label: Nothing to undo
tests.assertion: (() => { const l = new UndoableList(); l.undo(); return l.tasks.length === 0 })()

challenges.title: Expert: Show the list
challenges.promptMarkdown: Write `render(list, today)` that shows the tasks in four groups, in this order: `Overdue` (not done, due before today), `Today` (due today), `Later` (due after today) and `No date`, skipping empty groups. A task that is done and was due before today is left out. Each task is shown indented by two spaces as its `toString()`, then its tags as ` #tag`, then ` (DUE)` except in the Today group. Within a group, keep the order added. Show the sample list for `2026-11-12`.
challenges.hint: Work out a group name for each task with a small function. Then for each group name in order, filter the tasks, and show the heading and the lines if there are any.

tests.label: Shows the list
tests.assertion: _cq_prints("Overdue", "  [ ] Buy milk #home (2026-11-10)", "Today", "  [x] Send report #work", "Later", "  [ ] Book dentist (2026-12-01)", "No date", "  [ ] Read a book #home")

tests.label: Works with other data too

"✓" : "✗"} ${r.q.q} ${r.a ?? "—"}`); return _cq_prints(...lines, `Score: ${score(rows.map((r) => ({ correct: r.ok })))}`) })()

intro.title: An online shop's checkout
intro.bodyMarkdown:
The checkout is where an online shop earns its money, and where mistakes cost the most: a wrong total, a discount applied twice, or selling stock you don't have. Build one carefully, piece by piece.

The shop's server is played by an object `shop` with async methods, like a real API: `getProduct(id)`, `reserve(id, qty)` (which fails if there isn't enough stock) and `release(id, qty)` (to give stock back). You will write:

- a `Cart` class that adds products and works out the subtotal;
- discount codes read with a regex: `SAVE10` is 10% off, `TAKE5` is 5 off;
- the total with shipping, free from 50;
- loading a cart from the server, checking stock, and a **checkout** that reserves every line, or none of them if one fails;
- the receipt, with money formatted properly.

The last point matters: if the third line of an order fails, the first two must be **released** again, or the shop slowly "loses" stock nobody bought. Doing several steps as all-or-nothing is called a **transaction**, and undoing the done steps is a **rollback**.

```text
Mug            2 × €8.50       €17.00
T-shirt        1 × €19.99      €19.99
Pen            4 × €1.25        €5.00
Subtotal                       €41.99
Discount SAVE10                -€4.20
Shipping                        €4.50
Total                          €42.29
```

challenges.title: Easy: A cart
challenges.promptMarkdown: Write `class Cart` with an empty `lines` list and `add(product, qty = 1)`: if the product (same `id`) is already in the cart, add to its `qty`; else push `{ product, qty }`. Return `this`, so calls can be chained.
challenges.hint: `const line = this.lines.find((l) => l.product.id === product.id)`.

tests.label: Adds and merges
tests.assertion: (() => { const c = new Cart().add({ id: "mug", price: 8.5 }, 2).add({ id: "pen", price: 1 }).add({ id: "mug", price: 8.5 }); return c.lines.length === 2 && c.lines[0].qty === 3 && c.lines[1].qty === 1 })()

challenges.title: Easy: Subtotal
challenges.promptMarkdown: Add `subtotal()` to `Cart`: the sum of price × qty over the lines, rounded to cents.
challenges.hint: `reduce`, then `Math.round(sum * 100) / 100`.

tests.label: The sample cart
tests.assertion: (() => { const cart = new Cart()   .add({ id: "mug", name: "Mug", price: 8.5 }, 2)   .add({ id: "tee", name: "T-shirt", price: 19.99 })   .add({ id: "pen", name: "Pen", price: 1.25 }, 4) ; return cart.subtotal() === 41.99 })()

tests.label: Empty
tests.assertion: new Cart().subtotal() === 0

tests.label: Cents

intro.title: Plan your own project
intro.bodyMarkdown:
The best way to keep learning is to build something **you** want: a tracker for your training, a tool for your club, a game for a younger sibling, a page that shows data you care about. This last capstone is about **how** to do that well. The challenges walk through the process on an example, a habit tracker, so you can use the same steps on your own idea.

**1. Write down what it does, in a few sentences.** "I tick off habits each day. It shows my current streak for each habit and how I did this week." Anything not in those sentences waits for version 2. Small and finished beats big and half-done.

**2. Decide the shape of the data first.** Most of a program follows from it. Here: a list of `{ habit, date }` entries, dates as `YYYY-MM-DD` text. Plain data can be saved as JSON and checked by eye.

```
const log = [
  { habit: "read", date: "2026-11-09" },
  { habit: "read", date: "2026-11-10" },
  { habit: "run", date: "2026-11-10" },
]
console.log(JSON.stringify(log))
```

**3. Build the core as small functions that return values**, and try each one on a tiny example you can work out by hand. **4. Write tests** that check those examples, so that when you change something later you know at once if you broke something. A test can be as simple as a function that compares what you got with what you expected.

**5. Handle the bad cases**: missing data, a typo in a date, a server that is down. Decide what the user should see. **6. Add the outside world last**: the page, the buttons, saving, the network. Keep that part thin, and the core easy to test.

Then take your own idea through the same steps. When you get stuck, shrink the problem: get the smallest version working, then add one thing at a time. And read the error messages: they nearly always say what is wrong and where.
